articles.title: Re-acceleration in August
articles.heading: Swedish growth indicators
articles.fulltext:
Private sector production grew at a strong pace in August, re-accelerating after a slowdown in July.
 The monthly increase was 0.5%, in line with our forecast, but a revision to previous data lifted the year-on-year rate to 3.8%; somewhat higher than we had anticipated. Industrial production rebounded after a drop in July, bringing the year-on-year rate to a solid 5.8%. Monthly data are very volatile but the very positive underlying trend for the industry looks even stronger. New orders steadied following sharp swings in previous months, rising 5.5% y/y. Defence-related volatility in new orders is likely to continue ahead, as production and delivery of defense materials are often spread out over a number of years.
The GDP indicator came in at 1.1/3.5%
 - also in line with our forecast over the month but stronger on the yearly rate as previous numbers were revised higher. Most of the strong increases are reversals of weak readings in June and July and the average over July and August is largely unchanged compared to the average for Q2. The indicator thus signals weak quarterly growth in Q3, although this follows upon very strong growth in Q2. As we often point out, the monthly GDP indicator is highly volatile, often revised, and not necessarily a good indicator of actual growth. There are many signs of a broad-based, above-trend growth in Sweden, with sentiment indicators pointing to further strength ahead. Importantly, household consumption (August data published next week) is starting to increase more clearly. Some payback in Q3 is probable after the very strong Q2 (1.6%, 3.3% y/y), but both production and household consumption indicate upward risks to our Q3 forecast (0.2% q/q). 
We remain positive on the outlook for Swedish growth this year, seeing upside risks to our forecast that annual GDP will rise 2.7%.
 We forecast strong growth also in the coming year, but with households potentially hit by a cocktail of higher mortgage rates, higher energy prices and fading fiscal policy support, the growth outlook for 2027 might become considerably more subdued.

articles.title: CPI-ATE above Norges Bank’s forecast but slightly lower than expected
articles.heading: Norwegian inflation
articles.fulltext:
CPI-ATE was unchanged at 3.0%, slightly below our own and the consensus estimate but slightly above Norges Bank’s. Details were mixed with higher-than-expected food prices, but a relatively large decline for furniture prices worked in the opposite direction. We continue to see slightly higher core inflation than Norges Bank’s forecast in the next 3-6 months but predict slightly lower core inflation later in 2027.
Details: 
There were small differences for most items while there was a larger decline for other core goods, driven by furniture etc. Goods prices have been surprisingly high over the last 6-9 months, and this could be a bit of a payback. Stronger NOK should exert downward pressure on inflation over the next 12 months. Food prices declined less than normal. High food prices are a bit worrying, but food prices have been lower than expected since spring and volatility is high. Slightly lower service prices and rents are positive, but the deviations are small compared to monthly volatility.
Headline CPI increased to 3.4% from 3.3% y/y, which was 0.2-0.3pp lower than our forecast. As expected, fuel prices increased by almost 30% m/m, but electricity prices were unchanged and slightly below our forecast.
Implications Norges Bank:
 The downward revision to Norges Bank’s near-term trajectory (by 0.5pp) in its Sep26 MPR was surprisingly large. The 0.1ppt deviation in September (between consensus and Norges Bank’s estimate) should thus be rather neutral. However, we see a clear risk that the gap will widen in coming months. Though this will underpin current market pricing of a 50% chance for a Dec hike and a policy rate peak of 4.75%, we reiterate that we expect the policy rate peak to have been reached. Last year’s two rate cuts have now been reversed, and the Committee is clearly split on what’s deemed as a sufficiently restrictive policy. In the end, long-term inflation drivers will be decisive.

articles.title: Lower equities, lower oil prices, lower bond yields and lower AI revenues...
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
The US stock markets fell yesterday, with the S&P 500 ending at -0.5% and the Nasdaq at -1.5%. It is usually either concerns about rising interest rates, higher oil prices or AI that make markets gloomy. Yesterday, it was mainly AI concerns that drove the decline after the FT reported that OpenAI's annual revenue would be significantly lower than previously communicated. Oil prices initially climbed yesterday but fell back after Trump said he will not carry out any attacks on Iran before the midterm elections. U.S. long-term interest rates also fell back after an auction of 30y bonds went well with strong demand. With the return on bonds now as high as the expected return on the stock market (graph 
here
), it is hardly surprising that investors are starting to turn back to fixed income investments again.
France vs. the market. 
 The large deficits in the French budget have caused the markets to trade up the interest rate spread against Germany to levels not seen since the euro crisis in 2011 (graph 
here
). However, my personal view is that it is difficult to be too worried and that a situation where the ECB would have to step in with support measures is a long way off. France is a rich country that is fully capable of solving its own problems. But unpopular austerity measures does not happen by itself. It requires the market to force French politicians to make uncomfortable but necessary decisions. Hopefully, this is the process we are seeing in France now, even if all forms of austerity lead to large protests. In this context, it can also be noted, with some satisfaction, that the worst-hit countries during the previous European debt crisis, the PIIGS countries, have all today got their public finances in order (graph 
here
). If they can, so can France. 
In Asia
 , the stock markets are mixed today, with Japan at -0.3% and Hong Kong at +1.1%. Ahead of the opening here at home, both European and American stock market futures are pointing upwards. There have only been small movements in the foreign exchange market. 
Swedish data focus. 
 We have a lot of interesting Swedish economic statistics on the agenda today. Industrial production and the order situation should come in reasonably well if the strong industrial sentiment we have had in August and September is to be believed. The GDP indicator, which fell in July, should also have turned around in August. In Norway, focus will be on new inflation numbers.
Nordic key stories
The Swedish economy is doing well. 
 Yesterday, outgoing Finance Minister Elisabeth Svantesson painted a bright picture of the Swedish economy, which she predicts will grow by 3% this year and a decent 2.7% in 2027. According to the Finance Minister, a broad upturn is expected that includes both households and companies. At the same time, the assessment from August remains that the scope for reform is only SEK 50 billion for the entire coming parliamentary term.
Have a great Friday.

articles.title: Lägre börser, lägre oljepris, lägre långräntor och lägre AI-intäkter…
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Det var deppigt på USA-börserna igår. S&P 500 slutade på -0,5% och Nasdaq backade hela 1,5%. Det brukar ju vara antingen oro för stigande räntor, högre oljepris eller AI som får marknaden att tappa sugen. Igår var det framför allt AI-oro som drev nedgången efter att FT rapporterat att OpenAI:s årliga intäkter skulle bli betydligt lägre än vad som tidigare har kommunicerats. Oljepriset klättrade inledningsvis under gårdagen men föll tillbaka efter att Trump sagt att han inte kommer att genomföra några attacker på Iran innan mellanårsvalet. Amerikanska långräntor föll också tillbaka efter att en auktion av 30-åringar gått bra med stark efterfrågan. Då avkastningen på obligationer nu är lika hög som den förväntade avkastningen på börsen (graf 
här
) är det knappast förvånande att investerare börjar vända tillbaka till ränteplaceringar igen.
Frankrike vs. marknaden. 
De stora underskotten i den franska budgeten har fått marknaderna att handla upp räntespreaden mot Tyskland till nivåer som vi inte sett sedan eurokrisen 2011 (graf 
här
). Min personliga åsikt är ändå att det är svårt att bli alltför oroad och att ett läge där ECB skulle behöva gå in med stödåtgärder är långt borta. Frankrike är i grunden ett rikt land som är fullt kapabelt att lösa sina egna problem. Men impopulära åtstramningar kommer inte av sig självt utan det krävs att marknaden drar åt tumskruvarna och tvingar franska politiker att fatta obekväma men nödvändiga beslut. Det är förhoppningsvis den processen vi ser i Frankrike nu, även om alla former av åtstramningar leder till stora protester. I det sammanhanget kan man också, med viss tillfredställelse, notera att de värst drabbade länderna under den förra europeiska skuldkrisen, PIIGS-länderna, samtliga idag har fått ordning på sina statsfinanser (graf 
här
). Kan de så kan Frankrike även om det tar emot. 
I Asien
 är det blandat på börserna idag med Japan på -0,3% och Hongkong på +1,1%. Inför öppningen här hemma pekar både europeiska och amerikanska börsterminer uppåt. Det har bara varit små rörelser på valutamarknaden. 
Svenskt datafokus. 
Vi har en hel del intressant svensk konjunkturstatistik på agendan idag. Industriproduktion och orderläge borde komma in hyfsat om man ska tro det starka industrisentimentet vi har haft i augusti och september. Även BNP-indikatorn som backade i juli bör ha svängt om i augusti. För de som är intresserade av vad som händer i vårt västra grannland Norge kommer där nya inflationssiffror.
Sverige
Svensk ekonomi går som tåget. 
Igår målade avgående finansminister Elisabeth Svantesson en ljus bild av svensk ekonomi som hon spår kommer att växa med 3% i år och hyfsade 2,7% 2027. Enligt finansministern väntar en bred uppgång som omfattar både hushåll och företag. Samtidigt kvarstår bedömningen från augusti om att reformutrymmet bara är 50 mdr för hela den kommande mandatperioden. 
Ha en bra (om än regnig) fredag.

articles.title: Can the EU persuade China to reduce exports?
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
US stock markets fell yesterday, albeit modestly and from high levels. The price of oil (Brent) has risen by a couple of dollars to USD 102 per barrel following new Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and concerns that the US is preparing new attacks on Iran. US yields rose yesterday, but the increase eased after a government bond auction attracted decent demand. Asian stock markets are in negative territory overnight, while futures point to modest declines in Europe and the US ahead of today’s trading. Apart from US labour market statistics, today’s economic data calendar is relatively light, but there are numerous central bank speakers from the ECB (plus accounts from September meeting), the Bank of England and the Fed, as well as the Riksbank’s Thedéen and Norges Bank’s Bache.
Fed minutes – the rate peak has not been reached, but a pause in October.
 The minutes from the September 15–16 meeting showed that all members supported the rate hike and that most saw a need for further tightening before year-end. Several factors underpinned the assessment: inflation – both actual developments and concerns about it – was naturally in focus, but growth and the labour market also played a role. Although the message is hawkish, it is fully in line with the signals in Fed members’ own rate projections, which were released in conjunction with the meeting, and is less hawkish than market pricing at the time of the meeting and thereafter. Financial conditions were seen as supportive, but some members wanted to be prepared for risks of market dysfunction. We expect the Fed to pause in October and deliver one further 25-basis-point hike in December. Read our comment 
here
.
Can the EU persuade China to reduce exports?
 Today and tomorrow, the EU and China are discussing trade and investment in Beijing. From the EU’s perspective, China’s large trade surplus is unsurprisingly a key focus. One area in which the EU hopes to make progress is limiting imports of Chinese hybrid cars, which have increased sharply recently, partly as a result of the EU raising import tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. The fact that Germany and German carmakers are now pushing for import restrictions gives the EU greater weight on the issue, but China is reportedly opposed to such measures. Given China’s dependence on exports, the questions are how much it is prepared to concede, how far the EU can go unilaterally without provoking Chinese countermeasures, and whether a limited EU success would help or hinder the discussion on more extensive trade protection. The EU delegation will report back on the issue when the EU-leaders meet next week.
Recommended reading from us:
 An updated chart and analysis package on the war around the Persian Gulf (
here
), comments on the Norwegian government budget and fiscal policy (
here
), and industrial production (
here
).
Nordic key stories
Stronger trend in Swedish home prices.
 Data published by Svensk Mäklarstatistik this morning indicate a continued strong trend in the housing market. According to our own calculations, home prices have risen by almost 6% in total so far this year, or just over 3% on a seasonally adjusted basis. Revised data have removed some of the signs of weakness seen in recent months. A stronger trend is more consistent with our own home price indicator, the general improvement in consumer confidence, and the strong consumption data observed over the past six months.
Subdued underlying Swedish inflationary pressure despite high energy prices.
 Yesterday’s inflation figures were lower than expected for the second consecutive month. Energy prices are rising, but underlying inflationary pressure is more subdued. This supports our assessment that the higher inflation readings during the summer were partly temporary. This was the final inflation reading before the November rate decision. We expect the Riksbank to raise rates then, but the lower inflation readings may create some hesitation within the Executive Board. Read more

articles.title: Kan EU förmå Kina att minska exporten?
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
USA-börserna föll i går, om än måttligt och från höga nivåer. Oljepriset (Brent) har stigit ett par dollar till 102 dollar per fat efter nya Houthi-attacker mot Saudi Arabien och oro för att USA förbereder nya attacker mot Iran. USA-räntorna steg i går, men uppgången mattades av efter att en emission av statspapper mött god efterfrågan. De asiatiska börserna visar röda siffror under natten och terminer pekar på måttliga nedgångar i Europa och USA inför dagens handel. Utöver amerikansk arbetsmarknadsstatistik är dagens kalender relativt tunn på ekonomiska data, men innehåller desto fler centralbankstal från ECB (samt protokoll från septembermötet), Bank of England och Fed samt Riksbankens Thedéen och Norges Banks Bache.
Fed-protokollet – räntetoppen är inte nådd, men paus i oktober.
 Protokollet från mötet den 15–16 september visade att samtliga ledamöter stödde räntehöjningen och att flertalet såg behov av ytterligare åtstramning före årsskiftet. Flera faktorer låg bakom bedömningen: inflationen – både den faktiska utvecklingen och oron för den – stod naturligtvis i fokus, men även tillväxten och arbetsmarknaden vägde in. Även om budskapet är hökaktigt ligger det helt i linje med signalerna i Fed-ledamöternas egna ränteprognoser, som publicerades i samband med mötet, och det är mindre hökaktigt än marknadens prissättning vid mötestillfället och därefter. De finansiella förhållandena bedömdes vara gynnsamma, men några ledamöter ville ha beredskap för risker för störningar i marknadens funktionssätt. Vi räknar med en räntepaus i oktober och ytterligare en höjning med 25 räntepunkter i december. Läs vår kommentar 
här
. 
Kan EU förmå Kina att minska exporten?
 I dag och i morgon diskuterar EU och Kina handel och investeringar i Peking. Från EU:s sida står Kinas stora handelsöverskott föga förvånande i fokus. En delfråga där EU hoppas kunna göra framsteg är att begränsa importen av kinesiska hybridbilar, som har ökat kraftigt på senare tid, bland annat till följd av att EU höjde importtullarna på kinesiska elbilar. Att Tyskland och tyska bilföretag nu pressar på för importbegränsningar ger EU större tyngd i frågan, men Kina uppges motsätta sig sådana åtgärder. Mot bakgrund av Kinas exportberoende är frågan hur mycket landet är berett att ge med sig, hur långt EU kan gå unilateralt utan att Kina svarar med motåtgärder samt om en mindre EU-framgång hjälper, eller stjälper, diskussionen om mer omfattande handelsskydd. EU:s delegation ska återrapportera i frågan när stats- och regeringscheferna träffas nästa vecka.
Lästips från oss:
 Ett uppdaterat bild- och analyspaket om kriget kring Persiska viken (
här
), kommentarer om den norska statsbudgeten och finanspolitiken (
här
) samt industriproduktionen (
här
).
Sverige
Stark trend för bostadspriserna.
 Svensk Mäklarstatistik som publicerades nu på morgonen visar en fortsatt stark trend på bostadsmarknaden. Enligt vår egen sammanräkning har bostadspriserna totalt stigit med nästan 6 procent hittills i år, eller drygt 3 procent säsongsrensat. Reviderade utfall har tagit bort en del tecken på svaghet de senaste månaderna. En starkare trend ligger bättre i linje med vår egen boprisindikator, det generellt stärkta konsumentförtroendet och de starka konsumtionsutfall som vi har sett det senaste halvåret.
Dämpat underliggande inflationstryck trots höga energipriser.
 Gårdagens inflationsutfall var för andra månaden i rad lägre än väntat. Energipriserna stiger, men det underliggande inflationstrycket är mer dämpat. Det stödjer vår bedömning att sommarens högre inflationsutfall till viss del var tillfälliga. Detta var det sista inflationsutfallet före räntebeskedet i november. Vi tror att Riksbanken då höjer räntan, men de lägre inflationsutfallen kan skapa viss tvekan inom direktionen. Läs mer 
här
.

articles.title: Message in line with projections
articles.heading: Fed minutes
articles.fulltext:
The minutes from the September 15-16 meeting showed that all members supported the rate hike and that most assessed that another increase would likely be appropriate by year-end. While this is hawkish it is also fully in line with the signals in Fed members own rate projections that were released at the meeting and less hawkish than market pricing at the meeting and thereafter. Financial conditions were seen as supportive, but a few members wanted to prepare for the risks of market dysfunction. 
Key points
All members supported the rate hike, most believed another would be appropriate by year-end
Divergent views on policy stance and reasons for tightening
Financial conditions were seen as supportive because of equities and credit spreads
A few wanted to prepare for risks for treasury market dysfunction
Increased concerns for inflation but strong growth and improved labour market also had an impact on the decision
No surprises vs projections and somewhat outdated
Divergent views on policy stance and reasons for tightening 
While all members supported the rate hike, members were divided about why a higher policy rate was needed. Many saw it as an insurance against persistently high inflation, while a number thought it was necessary given their outlook. Presumably these are the same members who dissented in favour of a rate increase already at the July meeting. The minutes also reveal that members still have differing opinions about the degree of restrictiveness of current policy. “Several” stated that they did not see the current rate (before the September hike) as restrictive or only mildly restrictive. This suggests that other members are less sure about the degree of restrictiveness, which is in line with the view that a higher policy rate would be an insurance rather than motivated by their outlook. 
Supportive financial conditions, a few wanted to prepare for Treasury market dysfunction
The higher bond yields were thought to have been driven by stronger economic data, increased expectations for AI-related borrowing and geopolitics (i.e. energy prices). Interestingly, financial conditions were still seen as supportive by many participants due to rising equity prices and narrow credit spreads. At the same time, a few members expressed concerns about yields at the September meeting. Thus, “r
egarding balance sheet policy, a few participants observed that Treasury markets had been functioning smoothly but noted the importance of planning for market stress.” These members suggested “strengthening the Federal Reserve’s strategy, communications, and tools for addressing market dysfunction, should it occur, while limiting the Federal Reserve’s footprint in the Treasury market”.
Upside risks to inflation
The discussion showed that members had become more concerned about inflation, which is not surprising given the decision to hike and comments from Fed members both before and after the decision. Inflation had, according to minutes, 
remained elevated and members had not seen sufficient progress on lowering inflation in recent months. Ongoing geopolitical developments, which had pushed up prices for crude oil and refined fuel products, and surging AI-related investments were seen as contributing to inflation pressures. The minutes also highlight elevated core services prices excluding rents and elevated core goods prices, with the latter now pushed higher by the AI build-out while the impact of tariffs had faded. The possibility of further tariff increases was seen as an upside risk. 
Some members thought companies had become more successful in passing through higher costs to consumers. Some members thought risks to inflation had become more skewed to the upside in recent months. Many believed that the longer energy prices remained elevated, the larger the risks for spreading to other prices.
Larger than expected effect of new methods on core PCE, warnings about seasonal pattern
Members also discussed the effects of the upcoming new methods for PCE; these were expected by the Fed staff to lower core PCE by 0.2%-points in August (less than the actual decline of nearly 0.4%-points). A few participants “
observed that the 3-month change measure of core PCE inflation showed a material decline since the start of the year but cautioned that this measure is more volatil
e than the 12-month change measure and has shown a strong tendency to understate inflation in the second half of the year compared with the first half”. This could imply that members will hesitate to draw strong conclusions from the downside surprise in August and the fact that the 3-month change is now in line with the target. 
Strong growth and improved labour market also had an impact on the decision
In the discussion on monetary policy “participants generally emphasized that inflation remained elevated while the labor market appeared to be near full employment, with some signs of strengthening, and that economic activity was expanding at a solid pace. Almost all participants assessed that, while inflation risks were tilted to the upside, risks to the labor market had diminished and were now broadly balanced.” 
No surprises vs projections and somewhat outdated
All-in-all, we do not see minutes as surprising given the projections and other communication before and after the September decision. The outlook for rates is more cautious than market pricing at the time of the decision and after the meeting, but in line with the projections which indicated one or two more hikes. Strong growth data and an improved labour market appear to have played a role for the decision; it was not only about high inflation, and according to the minutes, future decision would depend on incoming information. It is also interesting to note the emphasis that members put on risky asset prices (equities and credit spreads) when judging financial conditions, which at least at the time of the meeting seemed to have outweighed the effects from rising yields in the view of the Fed.

articles.title: Budget broadly neutral for growth and Norges Bank
articles.heading: Norwegian fiscal policy
articles.fulltext:
The government’s budget proposal for 2027 implies a further increase in petroleum revenue spending to NOK 608bn. Due to continued growth in the oil fund, spending is unchanged at 2.7% of GPFG. The fiscal impulse is estimated to be marginally expansionary, though underscoring that overall fiscal demand impulses will ease in coming years. The budget proposal appears broadly in line with Norges Bank’s expectations and is thus unlikely to materially alter the near-term monetary policy outlook. Complicated negotiations await as the minority government needs support from four left-wing parties for its budget to be passed in Parliament. 
Overall conclusions:
 The 2027 budget proposal is broadly neutral from a fiscal-policy perspective and largely in line with expectations. The government signals some restraint, although petroleum revenue spending continues to rise. However, strong growth in the GPFG means spending will remain at 2.7% of the fund’s value. The Ministry of Finance’s macro models show a marginally positive contribution of 0.1-0.2ppt to mainland GDP. Considering that the government outlines a rather healthy economy with solid growth, low unemployment and still-high wage growth, one could argue that more restraint would have been desired. Broad-based tax cuts will underpin economic activity (and inflation), implying that fiscal policy will remain a complicating factor for Norges Bank. That said, spending appears broadly in line with Norges Bank’s expectations and is thus unlikely to materially alter the near-term monetary policy outlook.
The minority government needs support from four left-wing parties for its budget to be passed in Parliament. This will likely increase petroleum revenue spending slightly beyond what is estimated in this proposal. An amended budget will likely be approved by mid-December latest. 
Tax reforms:
 The budget proposal includes several tax adjustments. The government proposes personal tax reliefs in total of NOK 6.4bn by increasing the basic allowance and reducing social security contributions, providing broad-based support to households. The tax breaks in VAT related to electrical cars will be further scaled back, with the benefits scheduled to be fully phased out by 2028. This will help finance the income tax cuts. Subsidies related to the fixed-price electricity scheme “Norgespris” will continue, although the fixed-price will be increased marginally (from 0.40 to 0.45 NOK ex. VAT), still cushioning Norwegian household from high and volatile electricity prices. The budget proposes to raise the wealth-tax exemption threshold while maintaining the tax rate unchanged at 1% up to NOK 21.5mn in wealth and 1.1% on wealth above this.
Fiscal position:
 Norway’s fiscal position remains outstanding. The budget proposal puts the overall surplus at NOK 508bn in 2027, down from NOK 664bn in 2025, which corresponds to 8.6% of GDP. Excluding petroleum income, the government is running a deficit. The non-oil budget deficit is estimated to increase markedly by NOK 107bn to 562bn in 2027. In relation to mainland GDP, the non-oil budget deficit is estimated at 11.6% in 2027 vs. 9.9% in 2026.
Fiscal impulse:
 The structural non-oil budget deficit (i.e., actual petroleum revenue use) is estimated at a record high NOK 608.4bn, up from 583.4bn in 2026 (which has been lifted by NOK 4.4bn from the revised budget). Hence, the government plans to increase petroleum revenue spending by NOK 25bn next year, though measured in 2027-prices the increase is a more modest 4.9bn. This includes a support package to Ukraine of NOK 85bn which is unchanged from 2026. The fiscal impulse (i.e., the change in the structural deficit from one year to another) is estimated at 0.0ppt of trend mainland GDP vs. 1.1% in 2026. The Ministry of Finance thus concludes that the budget is “broadly neutral”, though its macro models suggest a slightly positive fiscal contribution of 0.1-0.2ppt.
Spending in relation to the fiscal policy rule:
 The fiscal policy rule states that petroleum revenue spending should equal the expected real return of the GPFG over a full cycle, set at 3%. The budget proposal puts spending at 2.7% of GPFG in 2027, unchanged from 2026. Considering optimistic growth projections and long-term challenges (e.g., demographics, increased spending related to demographics, defense and climate) spending should be well below the 3% rule. Moreover, increases in the oil fund’s value have been very large in recent years. In the start of 2027, the size of the GPFG is estimated to NOK 22400bn, an increase of 1100bn from 2026. The large increases in GPFG explain why fiscal spending, measured as the structural non-oil budget deficit, remains below the 3%-rule while spending has increased significantly in NOK amounts. To wit, funding from the GPFG is estimated to account for 26.6% of the budget and has increased markedly over the past years and stood at 21.5% in 2023.
Net cashflow from petroleum and oil prices:
 The government estimates net cashflow from petroleum (i.e., direct and indirect taxes, income from direct holdings and dividends) petroleum revenues of NOK 568.4bn in 2027, down from 670.6bn in 2026. Such income has gradually declined from the peak in 2022 when gas prices were historically high. Of the estimate for 2027, 58% is derived from petroleum taxes, 38.2% from the States Direct Financial Interest (SDFI) and 3.8% from dividends from Equinor. More specifically, petroleum taxes are estimated to decline by NOK 30bn to 359bn in 2026. Estimated income is based on an assumed average Brent oil price of NOK 803/bl (or 85 USD/bl) this year and NOK 703/bl (75 USD/bl) in 2027 as well as a gas price of 5.4 and 4.1 NOK/Sm3 in 2026 and 2027, respectively. 
Transfer to GPFG:
 Transfers to the GPFG were record-high in 2022-2023 owing to surging petroleum income, which has more than compensated for the large withdrawals during the pandemic. Transfers have moderated in recent years, and the government estimates a significantly smaller transfer of NOK 6.7bn in 2027 vs NOK 215.8bn in 2026. Meanwhile, income from the GPFG (e.g., interest rates and dividends) is expected to increase from NOK 460.2bn in 2026 to 515bn in 2027.
NOK purchases:
 As excess income is transferred to the GPFG and invested abroad, the government via Norges Bank is exchanging NOK-denominated petroleum income to FX before transferring income to the GPFG. However, petroleum revenues (which are used to fund the non-oil budget deficit) are denominated in both NOK (petroleum taxes, dividends from Equinor) and in FX (SDFI). What matters regarding the calculation of FX purchases is the non-oil budget deficit, not the structural one. There has been a large gap between the two deficits in recent years, explained by the trend/structural adjustments. For 2027, the non-oil budget deficit increases by NOK 106.9bn to 561.7bn. Hence, the actual need for NOK will increase relative to 2026. Meanwhile, petroleum tax income is expected to fall by NOK 30bn to 359bn. A simple equation by the budget proposal data suggests that there will be a need to buy NOK in the market to fund the deficit next year. In 2026, the budget also showed a NOK-buying need (which has then turned to NOK-selling due to higher petroleum tax income). As a comparison, revised 2026 numbers based on the new budget numbers imply an annual NOK need of approx. NOK 75bn in 2026 and 210bn in 2027.
NST borrowing:
 The structural non-oil deficit is always covered via a transfer from the GPFG, as issuance of government bonds is only allowed for funding of government lending schemes and to cover maturing existing debt. The borrowing requirement has been trending higher in recent years due to the maturity profile implying larger refinancing needs. However, the government seeks to avoid large swings in borrowing from year-to-year which is why Norges Bank has funded part of the increase by drawing on the government’s cash reserves. Since 2025, Norges Bank’s supply estimate has exceeded the underlying borrowing requirement with the aim of building up the cash reserves. For 2027, the underlying borrowing requirement is estimated to NOK 93.6bn vs. 95.7bn in 2026. And the Ministry of Finance states that a desire to maintain relatively stable borrowing from year to year could imply higher issuance than suggested by the requirement. Meanwhile, the government’s borrowing mandate in long-term debt is increased by NOK 50bn to NOK 200bn, providing greater flexibility and allowing for a potential increase in its own holdings. Overall, the budget proposal points to stable bond supply at around NOK 110bn, with risks tilted towards a modest increase.
Macro projections:
 The government presents a positive outlook for the Norwegian economy, despite global uncertainty as well as rising domestic price growth and interest rates expectations over the past six months. Mainland GDP growth has been revised down to 1.1% in 2026 and 1.7% in 2027 but remains above Norges Bank’s forecast of 0.9% and 1.0%, respectively. The government’s forecast for household consumption differs notably from Norges Bank’s: the government projects growth of 1.4% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027, compared with Norges Bank’s 0.8% and 2.6%. A higher wage growth forecast helps explain the government’s stronger consumption outlook this year: it expects annual wage growth of 4.6% in 2026, versus Norges Bank’s 4.4%. Norges Bank forecasts wage growth of 4.0% in 2027. The government also expects somewhat more persistent underlying inflation, with CPI-ATE unchanged at 3.1% in 2026 before easing marginally to 2.8% in 2027, this is 0.1ppt above Norges Bank’s 3.0% and 2.7% estimates, respectively. Registered unemployment is expected to remain stable at 2.1% in the coming years. Most importantly, spending equivalent to 2.7% of GPFG is in line with Norges Bank’s assumption in the Sep26 MPR. Hence, the budget proposal should not impact monetary policy near term.

articles.title: Continued reversal of high core inflation during summer
articles.heading: Swedish inflation
articles.fulltext:
Key points
CPIF ex energy in September was lower than we anticipated, for a second month in a row. Lower prices on services and food explains the difference compared to our forecast.
After three months of surprisingly high monthly increases, inflation has now been significantly lower than expected for two months in a row.
The Riksbank’s Executive Board has been clear in its signalling that a November rate hike is likely, and despite lower inflation, we expect the Riksbank to stick to the plan and hike on November 4. 
Core services and food lowered inflation in September
Despite sharply higher energy prices, underlying inflation pressures remain subdued. At 0.53% year-on-year, CPIF excluding energy was 0.16pp below our forecast and 0.21pp lower than the Riksbank’s estimate. Headline inflation was in line with the Riksbank’s forecast but slightly below our estimate, reflecting slightly higher energy prices than we anticipated. Adjusted for the lower VAT and subsidies for public transport, CPIF exe energy was unchanged at 1.5% y/y (SEB forecast 1.65% y/y, Riksbank 1.77% y/y) and the annualised and seasonally adjusted monthly price change was 1.1% m/m, well below target for a second consecutive month.
Core services and food prices explain the downside surprise compared to our estimate.
 The inflation rate for restaurant and hotels slowed to 2.2% y/y from 3.0% y/y, and we believe that a reversal of high hotel prices during the summer contributed to the slowdown. Other service prices also look lower than expected, but slightly accelerating pri
ces on recreation and similar imply that tourist service prices may have remained elevated in September.
Core goods (goods excluding energy, food, alcohol and tobacco) prices rose to 0.3% y/y, from -0.6% y/y. A weaker SEK is exerting upward pressure on goods prices and there are also some signs that prices on electronics continued to rise in September. 
The lower-than-expected core inflation supports our view that parts of the high inflation during the summer is temporary.
 We predict core inflation to rise gradually over the next 6-12 months, but short-term indicators do not support any major near-term shift in momentum. 
Headline CPIF will rise significantly driven by higher energy prices,
 mainly explained by reversal of the temporary tax cuts on fuels in Q4. Electricity prices in October have declined significantly and futures point to slightly lower prices also during the winter.
Policy implications:
September is the only inflation reading ahead of the November 4 rate decision. Strong signals in the September MPR for a rate hike in November implies that the Board will stick to its plan and deliver a hike in November, but the downside surprise in inflation should make at least some of the Board members considering waiting a bit longer. Markets continue to price a relatively high probability for hikes in both November and December, which looks excessive in our view. Growth indicators have continued to strengthen, suggesting that rate hikes are coming closer, but the Riksbank’s forecast for the labour market is in our opinion far too optimistic. 
We stick to our forecast for rate hikes in November, February and May but the combination of a downwards shift in expectations on rate hikes from the ECB and lower-than-expected inflation imply that near-term risks for the policy rate are skewed to the downside.

articles.title: Small decline in manufacturing production in August
articles.heading: Norwegian manufacturing production
articles.fulltext:
Manufacturing production fell by 0.4 % m/m in August, and the average in Jul-Aug is a modest 0.1% higher than the Q2 average. The 3m/3m rate has slowed lately and turned negative this month. Output growth was mixed between sectors; petroleum-related manufacturing dragged the overall figures down while traditional manufacturing basket limited the decline. Electricity output remains volatile, and the average so far in the quarter indicates a negative contribution to GDP in Q3. All in all, details are mixed and point to divergent contributions to the Q3 national accounts (due November). 
Manufacturing Production: 
Manufacturing production fell 0.4% m/m in August, with the Jul-Aug average 0.1% above the Q2 average, suggesting a mild to neutral contribution to manufacturing production in Q3. The year-on-year rate fell to 0.2%, from previously 1.4%. Traditional-related manufacturing (0.4% m/m) offered some support to the monthly figures while petroleum-related manufacturing production (-1.7% m/m) was a large drag. Within traditional-manufacturing production, wood and wood products rebounded (12.6% m/m) and lifted the figures, while the food, beverage and tobacco sector dragged the figures down, declining 1.2% m/m. Within petroleum-related manufacturing, ships, boats and platforms (-9.0% m/m) plummeted and was the largest drag this month, this comes after high activity with the sector in previous month. 
The average in Jul-Aug points to mild contribution to the quarterly figures and feeds into mainland GDP in Q3. The average so far in Q3 in output in manufacturing & mining is flat compared to the Q2 average, indicating a rather neutral contribution to mainland GDP in Q3 (due November), while electricity production will likely be a drag on growth in Q3, being 2.7% below the Q2 average. 
Separately, construction data rose marginally by 0.3% m/m in August, with a small upward move towards zero in the 3m/3m rate which has remained below zero for several years. Looking at the details, t
he largest category specialized construction activities lifted the monthly figures (1.1% m/m), while the second largest contribution from construction of buildings weighed on the figures (-0.2% m/m). Within this category, development of building projects declined (-1.9% m/m) whereas construction of residential and non-residential buildings was flat in August.
 Civil engineering declined 0.4% m/m. 
Industrial Production: 
Industrial production rose 1.0% in August, after a 7.1% decline (revised up from -7.6%) in the previous month. Industrial production is so far 2.3% lower than the Q2 average, driven by weak extraction and related services, suggesting that it will weigh on total GDP in Q3. Electricity declined for a second month in a row, though the 3m/3m remains positive at 6.8%.

articles.title: Swedish inflation set to rise; Fed minutes tonight
articles.heading: Nordic Alert
articles.fulltext:
Global key stories
Equity markets were all smiles yesterday and the S&P500 reached new highs against the backdrop of lower oil prices and falling bond yields. The krona strengthened broadly in the cheerful market sentiment, but has weakened a slightly during the morning as new Iranian attacks on oil tankers sent Brent oil (1st contract) above USD 100 per barrel again. Asian equity indices are down this morning (Nikkei -0.7%) and stock market futures point to lower opening prices in Europe and unchanged in the US.
In this week's Reflections
, Jens and Malte write about 
why long-term interest rates have risen
, and why the years of ultra-low interest rates should rather be seen as a historical parenthesis.
Busy agenda:
 among other things, Swedish inflation and budget balance, German and Norwegian industrial production, the Norwegian government budget proposal, an IMF speech – and not least, Fed minutes tonight.
German industrial production has been declining for several years
, but sentiment indicators indicate better times ahead. At the same time, many structural problems remain 
and in the near term, high natural gas prices are looming. In August, however, industrial production is expected to have risen after an unexpected fall in July.
Fed minutes in focus after hawkish September hike
. Fed members' own interest rate forecasts pointed to at least one further hike this year and probably another one in 2027, before rates can start to be lowered in 2028-2029. The minutes will be of particular interest for views on the need for more hikes, the extent to which inflation is driven by supply or demand factors, and how restrictive current monetary policy is. Several Fed members have recently signaled one or two further hikes, versus the three to four that the market has periodically priced in.
Nordic key stories
The Norwegian state budget for 2027 is presented today.
Norway has exceptional government finances with large oil and gas revenues. Spending is thus regulated by the so-called 3 per cent rule, which in simplified terms means that a maximum of 3 per cent of the value of the oil fund may be used in the state budget. However, the fund has grown to a somewhat fantastical NOK 22 trillion and the increase in value means that 
an additional NOK 24 billion
 can be spent without violating the rule. Fiscal policy is expected to continue to be expansionary, albeit less than in recent years. Central government spending in the 2026 budget was around NOK 2.2 trillion – more than twice as much per capita as in Sweden. Even considering that municipalities account for a larger share of spending in Sweden, Norway spends significantly more per capita (here until 2025). 
Very exciting Swedish inflation.
 We believe that core inflation (CPIF excluding energy) rose slightly in September, and that underlying inflation will increase gradually over the next six months. The weakening of the krona poses some upside risk to today's outcome, but continued reversal of high summer prices suggests that we could see a slight downside surprise today. On the other hand, large price increases for both electricity and fuel are expected to lift headline inflation clearly compared with August, and reduced subsidies and rising market prices mean energy prices will increase sharply in Q4. Read more in our 
Inflation Preview
.
SEB's survey, SEK Views, shows that respondents are still quite bullish on the SEK, but considerably less so than in March. 
The market is now considered to be heavily underweight SEK and EUR/SEK is expected to remain at 11.24 at the end of the year. The war in the Middle East remains a key risk, and the relatively tighter monetary policy abroad is expected to weigh on the krona over the next six months. Read more 
here.

articles.title: Stigande svensk inflation och Fed-protokoll
articles.heading: Morning Alert
articles.fulltext:
Internationellt
Det var muntra miner på börserna igår och S&P500 nådde nya högstanivåer mot bakgrund av lägre oljepris och sjunkande långräntor. Svenska 10-åringen stängde dock aningen högre efter stora nedgångar tidigare i veckan. Kronan stärktes på bred front i det glada marknadssentimentet, men har försvagats lite under morgonen efter att nya iranska attacker mot oljefartyg pressat upp priset på Brentolja över 100 dollar per fat igen. Asiatiska börsindex backar något under morgonen (Nikkei -0,7%) och börsterminer pekar på lägre öppningskurser i Europa och oförändrat i USA.
I Veckans Tanke
 skriver Jens och Malte om 
varför långa räntor stigit
, och varför åren med ultralåga räntor snarast ska ses som en historisk parentes.
Full agenda:
 bland annat svensk inflation och budgetbalans, tysk och norsk industriproduktion, norsk statsbudget, IMF-tal – och inte minst, Fed-protokoll ikväll.
Tysk industriproduktion har sjunkit under flera år
, men sentimentsindikatorer tyder på bättre tider framöver. Samtidigt kvarstår många strukturella problem (läs mer i Pias 
debattinlägg
) och i närtid hotar höga naturgaspriser att sätta käppar i hjulet. I augusti väntas industriproduktionen dock ha stigit efter ett oväntat fall i juli.
Fed-protokoll i fokus efter hökaktig septemberhöjning
. Ledamöternas ränteprognoser pekar mot minst en ytterligare höjning i år och troligen ytterligare en 2027, innan räntan kan börja sänkas 2028-2029. Protokollet blir framför allt intressant för synen på behovet av fler höjningar, i vilken utsträckning inflationen drivs av utbuds- respektive efterfrågefaktorer och hur åtstramande penningpolitiken bedöms vara. Flera Fed-ledamöter har på senare tid signalerat en eller två ytterligare höjningar, jämfört med de tre till fyra som marknaden periodvis prisat in.
Norsk statsbudget för 2027 presenteras idag.
 Norge har exceptionella statsfinanser med stora olje- och gasintäkter. Utgifterna regleras av den så kallade 3-procentsregeln, som förenklat innebär att högst 3 procent av oljefondens värde får användas i statsbudgeten. Fonden har dock vuxit till smått fantastiska 22 biljoner kroner och värdeökningen innebär att 
ytterligare cirka 24 miljarder NOK
 kan spenderas utan att bryta mot regeln. Finanspolitiken väntas fortsatt vara expansiv, om än mindre än de senaste åren. Statens utgifter i 2026 års budget var runt 2,2 biljoner NOK – mer än dubbelt så mycket per capita som i Sverige. Även med hänsyn till att kommunerna står för en större del av utgifterna i Sverige spenderar Norge avsevärt mer per invånare (här t.o.m. 2025).
Sverige
Mycket spännande svensk inflation.
 Vi tror att kärninflationen (KPIF exklusive energi) steg en aning i september, och att underliggande inflation ökar gradvis under det kommande halvåret. Kronförsvagningen utgör en viss uppåtrisk för dagens utfall, men fortsatt reversering av höga sommarpriser talar för att det skulle kunna komma en liten överraskning på nedsidan idag. Däremot väntas stora prisökningar på både el och bränsle lyfta totalinflationen tydligt jämfört med augusti, och minskade subventioner och stigande marknadspriser innebär ett kraftigt lyft för energipriserna inför fjärde kvartalet. Läs mer i Olles 
Morning Alert
 och i vår 
Inflation Preview
.
SEB:s enkät, Kronsyn, visar att synen på kronan har försämrats sedan i våras
, även om många fortfarande tror att kronan kommer att stärkas framöver. Marknaden bedöms nu vara kraftigt underviktad SEK och EUR/SEK väntas ligga kvar på 11,24 vid årsskiftet.
